newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech economy seen flat in first quarter.
newsitem.headline: Czech economy seen flat in first quarter.

text.p: Fresh figures on the troubled Czech economy should show little sign of growth for the first quarter, but no immediate easing of interest rates is likely in response, a Reuters poll of economists showed on Wednesday.
The Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) is scheduled to release first quarter GDP data at 0700 GMT on Thursday.

Analysts surveyed told Reuters that year-on-year GDP growth should be between zero and 0.5 percent, given earlier data showing a contraction in industrial and construction output for the quarter, and a lack of investment over the period.
"Anything below -1.0 percent growth and we could see pressure, between 0.0-1.0 percent would be good," said Boris Gomez, a macro-economic analyst at ING Barings in Prague.
"If it is lower than -1.0 percent, when people see the number it could really depress sentiment concerning the Czech Republic," he added.
First quarter year-on-year GDP growth in 1996 was 4.6 percent.
Analysts said that even if the figures were worse than expected, the Czech National Bank (CNB) appeared to be unwilling to ease its grip on interest rates to allow the economy room to breathe.

"The central bank is watching the crown, and that's all," said one London analyst. "It has shown that it is prepared to hold rates high, even at the cost of economic growth, to ensure currency stability."
At the end of May a speculative attack on the crown forced the central bank to raise its discount rate to 13 percent from 10.5 percent and the Lombard rate to 50 percent from 14 percent.

The CNB even cut off access to the Lombard lending facility as well as reaching an agreement with some local banks to keep non-residents out of the local money market and to restrain availability of crowns.
Over the past week, the central bank has removed the Lombard and money market restrictions, but has not touched either of its key rates.
On Tuesday Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus, who himself has predicted flat first quarter GDP figures, said high interest rates were depressing the economy and growth this year would be very low.
"It is depressing the economy already now and I understand the central bank is trying to make a soft landing," he told Reuters after a lecture at the London School of Economics.
"I take it (the current high interest rates) very seriously and I hope they (the rates) will not last long," he added.
The Czech economy recorded real growth of 4.4 percent in 1996, but a downturn in industry has sent economists scrambling to revise their forecasts downward.
On April 16, the government announced a series of economic measures aimed at reviving the economy while easing pressures from a burgeoning trade deficit and rising wages.
Klaus said then that he would consider it a success if Czech real GDP growth was 2.7 percent, half of the government's original estimate for 1997.
The crown crisis then pushed the government to act further, including cutting another 20 billion crowns ($624 million) from the budget and speeding up privatisation of some key sectors such as banks.
